headline: A Canadian province stops changing its clocks

sources.title: For thousands of workers, lifelong time-zone math will go out the window when B.C. stops changing clocks (CBC News)
Reactions mixed as B.C. to end time changes, adopt year-round daylight time (CBC News)
Adopting permanent daylight saving time (Government of British Columbia)

chunks.text: Most of the U.S. and Canada will {{fall back}} on Sunday, November 1, 2026. Clocks will move one hour earlier to [[standard time]], the normal winter time. But British Columbia, a [[province]] on Canada's Pacific coast, will not change its clocks. It will stay on [[daylight saving time]] all year. It is the time used in summer, when evenings stay light longer. The province is {{going ahead}} with the change [[on its own]].

verbs.correct: To set clocks one hour earlier
verbs.wrong: To end the workday one hour early
verbs.why: Clocks in most of the country fall back in November. We fall back and get one more hour of sleep. Most of Canada and the United States will fall back on Sunday, November 1, 2026.

verbs.correct: To do something that was planned
verbs.wrong: To ask people to vote on it
verbs.why: The game goes ahead even when it rains. If the weather is good, the school trip goes ahead. British Columbia is going ahead with year-round daylight saving time on its own.

chunks.text: The province's [[premier]], its elected leader, announced the plan on March 2, 2026. British Columbia passed a law for the change in 2019. But it {{held off}} for years, hoping nearby U.S. states would change too. The premier says when clocks change, children and parents lose sleep, and dogs {{get up}} at the wrong time. A 2019 [[public survey]] {{backed up}} the idea. Of 223,000 people who answered, 93 percent wanted daylight time [[year-round]].

verbs.wrong: To vote again on the same law
verbs.why: Many people hold off on buying a car until prices drop. She holds off on big decisions until she has all the facts. The government held off for years, hoping nearby American states would change too.

verbs.correct: To wake and start the day
verbs.wrong: To eat at a different hour
verbs.why: I get up at six on school days. My grandfather gets up early every morning. The premier says clock changes make dogs get up at the wrong time.

verbs.correct: To give support to an idea
verbs.why: New numbers often back up what doctors say. Good reasons back up a strong opinion. A 2019 public survey backed up the idea of daylight time all year.

chunks.text: In winter, British Columbia will be one hour ahead of Washington, the U.S. state to its south. Some workers for Canada's [[national government]] must change their hours to {{line up with}} eastern Canada or Washington. More than 100 [[call-center]] workers will work until 6 p.m., not 5 p.m. A [[union]] leader says some parents will {{end up}} needing more [[child care]]. A salesman says he will {{look up}} the time before meetings.

verbs.correct: To match the time of a place
verbs.wrong: To move to a new office
verbs.why: Our class times line up with the bus schedule. Her lunch break lines up with mine, so we eat together. Some workers must change their hours to line up with eastern Canada or Washington.

verbs.correct: To finally be in a situation
verbs.wrong: To ask for help from family
verbs.why: People who skip breakfast often end up hungry by ten. Many students end up with more homework than they expect. A union leader says some parents will end up needing more child care.

verbs.wrong: To write a note to a coworker
verbs.why: I look up new words in a dictionary. She looks up the bus times on her phone. A salesman says he will look up the time before meetings.

chunks.text: Reactions are [[mixed]]. In winter, the sun will {{come up}} one hour later than before. Skies could stay dark until 9 a.m. on the coast. A group for [[construction workers]] is worried about crews who start before [[dawn]]. Some scientists have {{spoken out}}, saying it could harm [[public health]]. The salesman is glad the changes will end, because they {{throw off}} his son's sleep. Most of the U.S. still changes its clocks. The premier hopes American neighbors will {{join in}} soon.

verbs.why: In summer, the sun comes up very early. The moon comes up over the hills at night. In winter, the sun will come up one hour later than before.

verbs.correct: To say what you think in public
verbs.wrong: To write a new science report
verbs.why: Parents often speak out when a school plans to close. Many doctors speak out about the dangers of smoking. Some scientists have spoken out, saying the change could harm public health.
Long flights throw off my sleep. A late dinner throws off the baby's bedtime. The salesman says clock changes throw off his young son's sleep.

verbs.correct: To become part of what others do
verbs.wrong: To meet to talk about a plan
verbs.why: When the music starts, everyone joins in and dances. My little brother always joins in when we play cards. The premier hopes American neighbors will join in soon.

mainIdea.s: British Columbia will skip the November clock change and keep daylight saving time all year. Many workers must change their schedules, and people have mixed feelings about the plan.
mainIdea.why: The province is going ahead with year-round daylight time on its own. Some workers must line up with new hours, and reactions are mixed.

mainIdea.s: Canada's west coast province is ending clock changes at the same time as Washington and California. Leaders say a shared move makes life simpler for families on both sides of the border.
mainIdea.why: Close, but British Columbia is going ahead on its own. Most of the U.S. still changes its clocks, so the province will be an hour ahead of Washington state.

mainIdea.s: British Columbia has moved its clocks forward by two hours to save energy in the winter. Officials expect the new time to help farmers who need more morning light for their crops.
mainIdea.why: The province will simply not fall back on November 1. It stays on daylight saving time, which is one hour later than standard time.

tf.s: British Columbia will not fall back with most of the U.S. and Canada.

tf.s: A public survey showed that most people wanted to keep changing clocks.

tf.s: Some workers must change their hours to line up with other places.
tf.why: Some workers for the national government must line up with eastern Canada or Washington.

tf.s: Every scientist supports the change and says it will help public health.

lines.text: Did you hear that British Columbia won't {{fall back}} on November 1?
Wait, they're keeping daylight saving time all winter?
Yes. They decided to [[go it alone]], without waiting for Washington or California.
Why now? I thought they passed that law years ago.
They did, in 2019. But they chose to {{hold off}}, hoping the U.S. would change too.
And most of the U.S. still changes its clocks.
Right. So in winter, British Columbia will be [[out of sync]] with Washington state.
That sounds hard for people who work across the border.
It is. Some workers have to {{line up with}} new hours, and parents may {{end up}} needing extra child care.
Do most people there like the idea?
Most did in 2019. A big survey {{backed up}} the plan.
But won't winter mornings be really dark?
Yes. The sun will {{come up}} later, so skies could stay dark until nine on the coast.
Imagine leaving home when it's [[pitch dark]]. I'd have trouble {{getting up}}.
It [[takes some getting used to]]. But one dad says clock changes {{throw off}} his son's sleep.
So a few dark mornings might be a [[small price to pay]].
Maybe. The premier hopes American states will {{join in}} soon.
Until then, I'll {{look up}} the time before I call anyone there!
